facts.statement: Patagornis lived during the Early to Middle Miocene epochs.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Early to Middle Miocene (Burdigalian to Serravallian)

facts.statement: The genus Patagornis was described by Francisco Moreno and Alcides Mercerat in 1891.
facts.quote: It was described by Argentine paleontologists Francisco Moreno and Alcides Mercerat in 1891.

facts.statement: Fossils of Patagornis were found in the Santa Cruz Formation in Santa Cruz Province, southern Argentina.
facts.quote: These fossils were unearthed by an expedition to strata (rock layers) of the Santa Cruz Formation in Santa Cruz Province, southern Argentina.

facts.statement: The Santa Cruz Formation, where Patagornis fossils were found, dates from approximately 17.5 to 11.6 million years ago.
facts.quote: This formation dates to the early-mid section of the Miocene, which makes it around 17.5 to 11.6 million years old.

facts.statement: In 1891, Florentino Ameghino named the species Tolmodus inflatus based on a premaxilla fragment.
facts.quote: Also in 1891, Moreno's scientific rival, Argentine naturalist Florentino Ameghino, named his own genus and species, Tolmodus inflatus, on the basis of a premaxilla fragment as well.

facts.statement: Some scientists continue to use the name Tolmodus instead of Patagornis despite Patagornis marshi being the correct name under ICZN rules.
facts.quote: Although, some scientists still use Tolmodus instead.

facts.statement: Patagornis had a tall and elongated skull similar to those of Andalgalornis and Andrewsornis.
facts.quote: Its skull is tall and elongated, similar to that of its kin Andalgalornis and Andrewsornis.

facts.statement: Patagornis is often considered the type genus of the subfamily Patagornithinae.
facts.quote: Patagornis is often regarded as being the type genus of its own subfamily, Patagornithinae.

facts.statement: Patagornis lived in southern Argentina during the Miocene in an environment of grasslands interspersed with forests.
facts.quote: Remains of Patagornis are exclusively known from the Miocene of southern Argentina, a region which was covered in grasslands, interspersed with forests, and contained a diverse array of reptiles, birds, and mammals when Patagornis lived.

facts.statement: Patagornis likely preyed on small to medium-sized mammals including the litoptern Thoatherium and the ground sloth Hapalops.
facts.quote: Patagornis potentially preyed on small-medium sized mammals such as the litoptern Thoatherium and the ground sloth Hapalops.

facts.statement: Patagornis may have competed with carnivorous sparassodont marsupials like Arctodictis and Prothylacinus for food.
facts.quote: Additionally, it may have competed with the carnivorous sparassodont marsupials Arctodictis and Prothylacinus for food.

facts.statement: The first Patagornis fossils were discovered by Museo de La Plata crews in the late 1880s.
facts.quote: The first known discovery of Patagornis fossils was made by crews of the MLP during the late 1880s.

facts.statement: The initial Patagornis fossil material consisted of a fragment thought to be a premaxilla, collected from the Santa Cruz Formation in southern Argentina.
facts.quote: The material, consisting of a mandibular symphysis (the area where the two mandibles meet) fragment, then thought to be from the premaxilla (the frontmost upper jaw bone), was collected from an unknown locality of the Santa Cruz Formation in Santa Cruz Province, southern Argentina.

facts.statement: The initial Patagornis fossils were originally thought to be from the Eocene but are now dated to the upper Middle Miocene.
facts.quote: Although then believed to be from the Eocene period, nicknamed the "Pyrotherium Beds", it is now thought to date to the upper section of the middle Miocene epoch.

facts.statement: Moreno and Mercerat formally described and named the species Patagornis marshi in May 1891.
facts.quote: In May 1891, Moreno and Mercerat scientifically described the remains and assigned them to a new genus and species of bird, which they named Patagornis marshi.

facts.statement: The genus name Patagornis combines 'Patagonia' and 'bird'.
facts.quote: The generic name Patagornis is a combination of Patagonia, where the fossils were discovered, and bird.

facts.statement: The species name marshi honors American paleontologist Othniel Charles Marsh.
facts.quote: The specific name is in honor of American paleontologist Othniel Charles Marsh, who made his own discoveries of fossil birds in the American West.

facts.statement: The mandibular symphysis fragment MLP-143 was designated as the lectotype for Patagornis marshi.
facts.quote: Later, the mandibular symphysis fragment (MLP-143) was selected as the lectotype (name-bearing) specimen of P. marshi.

facts.statement: Species P. lemoinei and P. bachmanni were originally named by Moreno and Mercerat but were later moved to the genus Psilopterus.
facts.quote: However, they were unearthed in lower Miocene rocks of the Monte León Formation and have since been moved to the genus Psilopterus.

facts.statement: The genus Morenomerceraria is now considered a synonym of Patagornis marshi.
facts.quote: However, it is now considered a synonym of Patagornis marshi.

facts.statement: Florentino Ameghino described the genus Tolmodus in August 1891 based on a premaxilla fragment.
facts.quote: In August 1891, Ameghino scientifically described a new genus and species of phorusrhacid (then incorrectly spelled "phororhacid") bird (though at the time he believed it was a megalonychid sloth), Tolmodus inflatus, on the basis of a premaxilla fragment.

facts.statement: Ameghino classified Tolmodus within the family Phorusrhacidae in 1895.
facts.quote: In 1895, Ameghino classified Tolmodus in Phorusrhacidae.

facts.statement: Alvarenga and Höfling revalidated the name Patagornis in 2003, treating Tolmodus as a junior synonym.
facts.quote: In 2003 Brazilian paleontologist Herculano Alvarenga and German paleontologist Elizabeth Höfling opted to revalidate the name Patagornis and considered Tolmodus a junior synonym (the same taxon as a previously named taxon).

facts.statement: There is little scientific consensus on whether Tolmodus or Patagornis is the correct generic name for the animal.
facts.quote: The use of both Tolmodus and Patagornis is prevalent in scientific literature, with little consensus on what is the correct generic title.

facts.statement: John Bell Hatcher led Princeton University expeditions to Santa Cruz Province between 1896 and 1899.
facts.quote: Between 1896 and 1899, Princeton University students, under the leadership of American paleontologist John Bell Hatcher, led a series of expeditions to the same outcrops in Santa Cruz Province.

facts.statement: Sinclair and Farr described new phorusrhacid material in 1932, assigning it to Pelecyornis and Phorusrhacos.
facts.quote: In 1932, Sinclair and Farr described the newly found phorusrhacid material in detail, assigning much of it to Pelecyornis (a synonym of Psilopterus) and Phorusrhacos.

facts.statement: Barnum Brown discovered an associated postcranial skeleton 10 miles north of Cape Fairweather in Santa Cruz.
facts.quote: From a locality 10 miles north of Cape Fairweather, Santa Cruz, American paleontologist Barnum Brown unearthed an associated postcranial skeleton from a phorusrhacid (AMNH 9264) consisting of an incomplete pelvis, right femur (thigh bone), tibiotarsus (shin bone), tarsometatarsus, and pes (foot).

facts.statement: An MLP expedition in February 2020 found an isolated Patagornis metatarsal fragment in the Cerro Boleadoras Formation.
facts.quote: In February 2020, an expedition by the MLP to outcrops of the middle Miocene-aged Cerro Boleadoras Formation unearthed a multitude of fossils, including an isolated metatarsal fragment of Patagornis.

facts.statement: Patagornis had small abdomens and wings relative to its long, lithe hindlimbs.
facts.quote: The abdomen and wings are small in contrast to the long, lithe hindlimbs.

facts.statement: Patagornis stood approximately 0.9 to 1 meter tall at the back and weighed between 45 and 50 kilograms.
facts.quote: Patagornis was about 0.9-1 m tall at the back and 45-50 kg in mass.

facts.statement: The skull of the most complete Patagornis specimen measures 33.7 cm in length and 12 cm in width.
facts.quote: Its skull measures 33.7 cm in length from occipital to the end of the premaxilla and 12 cm at its greatest width.

facts.statement: Patagornis nostrils were relatively tall with a high peak on the dorsal side, unlike other phorusrhacids.
facts.quote: The dorsal (top) side of the nostrils is relatively tall with a high peak, unlike those of other phorusrhacids.

facts.statement: The specimen NHMUK PV A516 is one of the few phorusrhacid skeletons that preserves the hyoid apparatus.
facts.quote: NHMUK PV A516 is one of the few phorusrhacid specimens that preserves the hyoid.

facts.statement: The leg bone ratio in Patagornis suggests it was a very agile animal.
facts.quote: At Patagornis this ratio is almost 70%, meaning that the taxon was very agile, a trait common among the smaller Patagornithines.

facts.statement: Research from 2005 estimated Patagornis had a maximum running speed of 50 km/h.
facts.quote: Research from 2005 therefore showed that the animal had a maximum speed of 50 km/h, about the same speed as the living rhea.

facts.statement: Researchers estimated Patagornis could run at a speed of 14 m/s based on the strength of its shin bone.
facts.quote: The tibiotarsal strength of Patagornis and an indeterminate large phorusrhacine suggested a speed of 14 m/s

facts.statement: Scientists suggest Patagornis likely used its strong legs to break the bones of medium-sized mammals rather than for high-speed running.
facts.quote: They found these estimates unlikely due to the large body size of these birds, and instead suggested the strength could have been used to break the long-bones of medium-sized mammals

facts.statement: Researchers hypothesize that Patagornis may have used its beak and claws to attack well-armored mammals like armadillos and glyptodonts.
facts.quote: They also suggested future studies could examine whether they could have used their beaks and claws against well-armored mammals such as armadillos and glyptodonts

facts.statement: Fossils of Patagornis preserve large, spur-like quill knobs on the ulna that likely served as attachment points for long feathers.
facts.quote: NHMUK PV A 516's ulna preserves large, spur-like quill knobs on the posterior end that may have been the attachment point for elongate feathers

facts.statement: Theories suggest Patagornis used its elongate feathers either to assist in running or as a defensive shield similar to the secretarybird.
facts.quote: These feathers were theorized to have been used for assistance in running, as implied by its ecology and limb anatomy, or as a shield like those of the secretarybird

facts.statement: Patagornis possessed large, curved, and laterally thin toe claws that were likely used to stab prey, similar to modern predatory birds.
facts.quote: The ungual phalanges preserved in Patagornis and its distant relative Mesembriornis are large, curved, and thin laterally, likely being used to stab prey based on those of modern predatory birds

facts.statement: Studies of ear anatomy reveal that Patagornis had poor hearing with the smallest hearing range among the Cariamiformes examined.
facts.quote: They discovered that Patagornis had poor hearing, the smallest hearing range in the Cariamiformes studied

facts.statement: Due to its body mass, Patagornis likely exhibited sluggish head movements but had enhanced sensitivity to low-amplitude motions.
facts.quote: with the greater body mass, it was inferred that there were more sluggish head movements in this taxon, with enhanced sensitivity to low-amplitude motions

facts.statement: Bone histology suggests Patagornis reached sexual and skeletal maturity before achieving full somatic maturity.
facts.quote: This implies that Brontornis and Patagornis may have reached sexual and skeletal maturity prior to somatic maturity

facts.statement: Fossils of Patagornis show a smooth outer bone texture, indicating the specimens were fully grown individuals.
facts.quote: The fossils studied indicated they came from fully grown individuals based on the presence of a smooth outer bone texture, which is a signifier of skeletal maturity

facts.statement: Patagornis exhibited an uninterrupted growth pattern, possibly resulting from living in unstable continental environments.
facts.quote: Patagornis and Brontornis had an uninterrupted growth pattern which may have been a consequence of living in stochastic, continental environments

facts.statement: Mercerat established the family Patagornithidae in 1897 to group Patagornis and Pelecyornis based on shared features of their humeri and tarsometatarsi.
facts.quote: In 1897, Mercerat erected the family Patagornithidae for Patagornis and Pelecyornis (a synonym of Psilopterus), which were united by features of their humeri and tarsometatarsi

facts.statement: The name Patagornithidae was revalidated as the subfamily Patagornithinae in 2003 by Alvarenga and Höfling after remaining unused in scientific literature.
facts.quote: However, the name went unused in scientifici literature until 2003, when Alvarenga and Höfling revalidated it as the subfamily Patagornithinae

facts.statement: Alvarenga and Höfling defined the subfamily Patagornithinae in 2003 as a clade of medium-sized birds with long, narrow mandibular symphyses and slender tarsometatarsi.
facts.quote: In their 2003 study, Alvarenga and Höfling defined Patagornithinae as the clade including Patagornis and its closest kin, which were united by their medium sizes, long, narrow mandibular symphyses, long, slender tarsometararsi, and overall comparatively smaller, lither build than phorusrhacines

facts.statement: A 2025 study by Agnolín and colleagues proposed that Patagorhacos is a close relative of Patagornis.
facts.quote: In 2025, Agnolín and colleagues suggested that the other phorusrhacid Patagorhacos was a close relative of Patagornis

facts.statement: Moreno and Mercerat first described the species in May 1891 under the name Patagornis marshi.

facts.statement: In June of the same year, Ameghino described material of this species with the name Tolmodus inflatus.
facts.quote: pero en junio del mismo año Ameghino describe material de esta especie con el nombre Tolmodus inflatus

facts.statement: According to the principle of priority, the valid name is Patagornis marshi because it was described a month before the alternative name.
facts.quote: Por norma de prioridad nomenclatural el nombre válido es Patagornis marshi, al haber sido descrito un mes antes

facts.statement: While most researchers accept Patagornis marshi as correct, a few still prefer the name Tolmodus inflatus.
facts.quote: En la actualidad la mayoría de investigadores aceptan como correcto el nombre Patagornis marshi, pero unos pocos aún prefieren el nombre Tolmodus inflatus

facts.statement: It is a small terror bird, up to 15% larger than a modern rhea.

facts.statement: Fragmentary remains have been described from the Cerro Boleadoras Formation, dating between 16.5 and 15.1 million years ago.

facts.statement: These formations correspond to the Santacrucian SALMA, dating to the early Miocene stage between 18 and 14 million years ago.

facts.statement: A 2012 study suggested phorusrhacids could not hunt prey larger than themselves, but later studies countered this by noting extant birds can hunt significantly larger prey.
facts.quote: Although in a 2012 study, Argentine paleontologist Federico Degrange suggested that phorusrhacids were incapable of hunting prey larger than themselves due to their dependency on head, neck, and hindlimb movement, later studies have countered this by stating that extant birds have proven they can hunt prey significantly greater than themselves

facts.statement: The tarsometatarsus of Patagornis marshi is approximately 70% the length of the tibiotarsus, indicating an agile lifestyle adapted for speed.

facts.statement: The short and robust auditory canals in the skull of Patagornis marshi suggest sensitivity to low-amplitude movements, evidence that it executed slow head strikes when attacking.
facts.quote: Se conoce también que los canales auditivos en el cráneo de Patagornis marshi eran cortos y robustos, lo cual sugiere sensibilidad a movimientos de baja amplitud, evidencia de que al momento de atacar ejecutaba golpes lentos de cabeza.
